(1) the problem of determining a robot’s position in a graph is equivalent to the problem of determining the shortest path from a source to a target in the graph, and (2) the problem of navigating to the target in the graph is equivalent to finding the shortest path from the current position to the target.
(i) the robot’s knowledge of the graph can be reduced to a set of landmark distances, and (ii) the robot can use these distances to compute its current position.

the robot’s ability to localize is dependent on its ability to detect landmarks and the number of landmarks it can see at any given time, and that the robot’s performance is dependent on the number of landmarks that are used for localization.

the design of algorithms for a robot to locate itself in a graph space by the use of a set of landmarks, and with the study of properties of the graph that are important in this context.
the problem of determining the robot’s position in a graph space, given the distances from a robot’s position to a set of distinctively labeled landmark nodes.
the problem of navigation in a graph-structure environment by a robot with distance sensors.
